tip: During your takeaway, keep your hands close to your body — push the club straight back without letting your arms drift away. The moment your path strays even slightly, club speed will decelerate. Memorize this correct path and never deviate from it.

As you complete your backswing, fold your right arm so that your right elbow points down toward the ground. This keeps the right arm connected to your body and prevents it from flying out, giving you a solid, repeatable structure at the top.

At the top of your backswing, angle your right palm approximately 45 degrees — this creates a slight bowing of the lead wrist, which is what the best players on tour are doing today. Avoid excessive cupping of the wrist at all costs, as it destroys your swing plane.

On the downswing, don't initiate the movement with your shoulders or body rotation. Instead, feel like your hands and right arm are dropping straight down toward the ball along the same path they went up — think of it as one connected unit coming down on plane.

Don't drag or force your wrists through impact — instead, let the wrists release naturally and freely, like you're throwing the clubhead into the ball. Think of the club as a very heavy axe and simply let gravity drop it down the correct path.

If you're doing this correctly, you'll feel the clubhead become noticeably heavier than you've ever felt it before — especially as your hands approach the ground near impact. That sensation of heaviness is proof you're on the right path and accelerating through the ball.

After you release the clubhead through impact, use your lower body to drive through to a full finish. The sequence must be: takeaway, fold the right arm, drop it down, release the head, then rotate through with your lower body — follow this order every single time.

Stop thinking about pulling the club down toward your body on the downswing — that is the worst feeling you can have. Instead, imagine a cable attached to the clubhead and push it away from you, as far out as possible, as you start down. This keeps the arc wide and lets you generate real power.

When you pull the handle toward your body coming down, the clubhead wants to come over the top and the path gets steep — you lose all your space and power. Feel like the clubhead is swinging away and out, not being dragged in, and the shaft will shallow out naturally, very similar to the shallowing sensation.

The armpit drill — keeping a pen or ball squeezed in your armpit — only makes sense for more advanced players who already have a wide, connected swing. For beginners, it can actually encourage pulling the arms too tight to the body and steepening the swing, so avoid it until you have the fundamentals down.

The 'vertical drop' feeling everyone talks about is not about yanking the arms straight down — it is about letting the club simply fall, right here, from the top, with no extra effort. Just drop it and let your body rotate; that passive drop is what creates the correct downswing path.

Your wrist hinge — your cock — must release at impact, no exceptions. When you drop the club passively and rotate, the hinge releases naturally. If you try to hold the angle and drive the handle forward with your shoulders and arms, the club stays steep, the face goes open, and you end up shanking or slicing.

Real shaft lean at impact does not come from pushing your hands forward — it comes from your body rotating through while the clubhead naturally lags behind. Drop the club, let the wrists release freely, and trust the rotation to create the forward lean; forcing it by pulling the handle just causes hooks and fat shots.

Golf is about hitting the ball with the weight of the clubhead, not muscling it with your arms. If you are gripping tight and dragging the club down, you will never feel that weight. Let the club drop freely — the moment you feel the head's weight swinging, you have found the right sensation and distance will take care of itself.

After you drop the club passively, you must shift your weight hard to the left side — think of pressing into a wall on your lead side. If you spin in place instead of shifting, you will hit it fat every time; but if you start hitting fat shots after practicing the drop, that actually means you are halfway there — now just add that left-side push.

Most slicers fall back at impact because their steep downswing forces the body to retreat to find the ball. Once you shallow out the drop and stop pulling the club steep, there is no reason to fall back — commit to the left-side shift and the compensation disappears along with the slice.

Most golfers leave long putts short about 80% of the time without even realizing it. Instead of aiming at the hole, set your target 30cm (about one foot) past the cup so you always give the putt enough speed to reach and hold its line.
Stop staring at the ball before you putt — that kills your distance feel. Fix your eyes on your target for a full 3 seconds, then stroke immediately while that image is fresh in your mind.

A putt that dies 30cm past the hole uses the full width of the cup — even an off-center hit can fall in. Hit it harder than that and only a dead-center strike will drop, so always aim for that 30cm-past pace to maximize your effective target size.

If your putts keep missing right, especially on downhill sliders, check your left armpit — when it separates from your body, the putter face opens through impact. Keep both armpits pinned close to your sides throughout the stroke to keep the face square.

After every missed putt, note not just that it missed, but which direction and whether it was short or long. Tracking your personal miss pattern — short, long, left, or right — gives you actionable feedback that compounds over every round and steadily lowers your putting average.

Feel the weight of the clubhead by simply dropping it toward the 3 o'clock position on the downswing. Don't force it — just let gravity pull the head down, and it will naturally swing up through the follow-through on its own. If you can feel that drop, golf becomes much easier.

Casting and scooping happen because your body rotates too early, throwing the club forward and out in front of you. Instead of trying to fix it by pulling the club through with force, learn to release your grip tension and let the club drop freely — fighting the cast with more force only makes it worse.

To shallow the downswing naturally, keep your back turned to the target as you start the downswing and drop the club toward the 3 o'clock position. When your back stays loaded and facing away, it becomes physically impossible to come over the top — the shallow path happens automatically.

Your arms and body need to separate at the start of the downswing — the arms drop first while the body stays back, not the other way around. When everything moves together as one unit, you lose all sense of clubhead weight and the release becomes impossible to time correctly.

Loosen your grip to the point where you feel like you might actually drop the club — that is the correct feeling you are looking for. Grip tension is the number one thing that kills the natural release, so practice swinging with almost no hand pressure until you feel the clubhead swinging freely on its own.

When you try to drop the club toward 3 o'clock but your weight stays on the wrong side, your body flips and tips over rather than rotating through. Pair the arm drop with a proper weight shift to the left side — the drop and the weight transfer must happen together for the move to work correctly.

Stop trying to hit the ball — instead, focus on dropping the club's weight down and letting that momentum carry all the way through to the target. Think of it like snapping a wet towel: the power comes from relaxed acceleration, not from smashing at a specific point.

You do not need to artificially hold the lag angle — if your hands are relaxed and moving with speed, the lag will create itself for free. The clubhead naturally lags behind loose, fast-moving hands, so focus only on softening your grip and increasing hand speed, and the lag will appear on its own.

Once you have learned to drop the club freely with soft hands, add lower body movement by shifting your weight to the left side — do not rotate the hips, just transfer the weight. Time the weight shift to coincide with the moment the clubhead reaches its lowest point for maximum efficiency.

Imagine snapping a towel with your shoulders completely relaxed and hanging loose — that is exactly the feeling you need in your downswing. Drop the arms from a relaxed shoulder position and let the speed build naturally from that looseness, not from muscling through with a tight upper body.

At impact, don't try to forcefully straighten your left arm — that tension is what causes the arm to block and the shoulder to stall. Instead, feel like your left arm is simply releasing away from your body, like throwing a boomerang. That relaxed, separating motion is the foundation of a clean impact.

If your left shoulder is blocking or you're thrusting your hips into the ball at impact, no amount of other coaching will fix your ball-striking. The root cause is usually too much tension in the left arm causing it to over-extend. Fix the arm motion first, and the early extension will naturally disappear — don't try to suppress the thrust directly.

Rotating your upper body more is not the solution when your left shoulder is stalling — I tested it and the arms still can't reach full extension. What actually allows the arms to extend properly is lower body rotation below the navel. Trying to force rotation with an upper body full of tension just creates a wild, spinning swing with no speed and no direction.

The correct sequence is: first, learn to separate the left arm and armpit so the arm can move freely with relaxed shoulders — then, and only then, add lower body rotation to accelerate. If you try to use the lower body before the arm motion is correct, you'll spin out and lose all control and power.

Practice swinging as if you are throwing a boomerang with your left arm — the arm releases away from the body naturally and freely. Don't worry about where the ball starts going at first; just repeat this feeling of the left arm separating and releasing through impact. Once this motion is grooved, your body rotation will become far more effective.
If your ball is consistently going left, check for a reverse pivot in your backswing. A reverse pivot dramatically increases the chance of pulling the ball left on every shot.

Stop artificially pressing your left shoulder down on the downswing — this is a very common but damaging habit. The moment you force that shoulder down, your swing path opens and the ball flies hard to the left every time.

When you press the left shoulder down at the start of the downswing, the club approaches from outside the target line and you end up hitting over the top. The clubhead needs to come from the inside — keep your upper body back and let the lower body lead.

If you are upper-body dominant, first learn to swing freely with your arms and get rid of the tension in your upper body. Only once that tension is gone should you start working on lower body separation — trying to separate too early will just cause everything to move together.

On the downswing, don't immediately rotate your hips — instead, laterally shift them toward the target first. Think of pushing your left hip sideways, not spinning it, so the club can drop to the inside and approach the ball on the correct path.

In the downswing sequence, keep your upper body back while your lower body begins to move — the upper body should only unwind because the lower body forces it to. If both move at the same time, you lose all the rotational power and the club gets thrown outside.

Place a shaft or stick near your lead shoulder at the top of the backswing. If your upper body rotates early on the downswing, you will hit the stick — use this as instant feedback to train yourself to keep the upper body back while the hips shift first.

When you first fix the over-the-top move, you may start hitting fat shots — that is normal. To correct it, focus on moving your hands forward in front of your body at impact rather than using your shoulder to avoid the ground.

Place a strip of tape on the ground about one hand-width behind the ball. Practice swinging with the sole intention of NOT hitting that tape — this trains your low point to be in front of the ball and builds the feeling of a forward-leaning shaft at impact.

When you see tour players with their left shoulder appearing low through impact, that is not because they are pressing it down — it is because they are maintaining their spine angle while shifting their weight, so the shoulder simply stays lower naturally. Pressing it down yourself is a completely different and harmful movement.

There is a big difference between a lateral weight shift and a sway — do not confuse them. Shift your hips toward the target in the one o'clock direction, but never let your weight fall backward or your body tip over. The shift should load your left side, not your right.

Ground reaction force — pushing off the front foot to generate speed — is an advanced skill. For now, just focus on shifting your weight to your left side smoothly. Master the lateral shift first, then learn to push off the ground for extra clubhead speed later.

Keep your backswing simple: rotate fully, then push your hips laterally toward the target to start the downswing. That is all you need to think about — a consistent backswing rotation followed by a lateral hip push, then let the swing finish naturally.

If you lack flexibility, forcing a big backswing will almost always cause you to come over the top. Instead, keep your backswing low and compact — focus on sweeping the club back close to the ground to naturally create an in-to-out swing path.

The real power in your swing comes from your hip slide and rotation through the downswing — not from your arms. Drive your hips through impact and let that rotational energy release naturally into your follow-through.

Golf is not about how strong you are — it's about using the weight of the clubhead and proper weight transfer to generate distance. Even the biggest hitters rely on technique, not brute force, to make the ball go far.

Ask yourself: what is the single most necessary movement for me to score well? More often than not, the answer is a simpler motion, not a more complex one. Strip away unnecessary movements and focus only on what your body actually needs.

Before you swing, feel the weight of the clubhead — this awareness is key to maximizing distance and consistency. When you stay connected to that weight throughout your swing, you stop muscling the shot and start swinging with real efficiency.

With the driver, keeping too much wrist hinge through the downswing creates a steep angle of attack, causing the clubhead to arrive too far ahead of its proper path. This forces you to either flip the hands aggressively and pull the ball left, or leave the face open and push it right. Release the wrist angle early and freely on the downswing to shallow out your swing plane and give yourself room to rotate through impact.

When the driver swing is too steep, many golfers instinctively hang back and spin the body to avoid hitting right — but this just creates more inconsistency. Instead of pulling away from the ball, focus on releasing the wrists early to shallow the path, then rotate and shift your weight to the left side through impact.

Unlike irons, the driver has a much flatter swing arc, so holding onto your wrist hinge into the downswing will make the club come in too steep and cause thin or pulled shots. Let the wrists release freely — more than feels comfortable at first — and you'll find the clubhead naturally approaches from a shallower, more powerful angle.

Practice this drill: grip down to the very bottom of the handle, take your backswing, then feel like you are dropping the club down toward your right heel twice — 'thud, thud' — before sweeping it upward toward the sky. This two-stage drop-then-lift feeling trains you to shallow the club and approach the ball on a wide, sweeping arc rather than a steep chop.

If you are hitting fat shots when practicing the early wrist release, it is because your body is reverting to its old habit of hanging back instead of shifting left. As you sweep the club upward through impact, make sure your body moves with it — feel like you are scooping water up and to the left, transferring your weight forward at the same time.

When learning the early wrist release with the driver, start by choking down to the very bottom of the grip so the club is easier to control and you are less likely to hit fat. Once the movement feels natural, gradually move your hands up the grip about 2 cm at a time until you reach your normal full-grip position.

Stop letting your upper body rise up just before impact — when you stand up early, you lose all connection to the ground and end up hitting with nothing but arm strength. Keep your spine angle maintained through impact so your lower body can actually do its job.

You need to feel the ground pushing back against you at impact — that's ground reaction force, and it's what separates real power from arm-only swings. Practice staying connected to the ground through the hit, and you'll be shocked how much more distance you can generate with less effort.

Your hips should feel like they're staying folded and loaded through impact — the moment your hips extend and straighten early, you've lost the shot. Think of keeping that hip crease held as long as possible rather than thrusting or rotating them open too soon.

Imagine there's a big balloon sitting right in front of your belly, and your only job is to not pop it — this keeps your chest and torso from flying open before impact. Your chest laser should stay pointed at the ball all the way through contact, not up at the sky.

When your body stays down and your spine angle holds, your left arm can release freely and fast — but the moment your body rises, the left arm gets trapped and can't get through. Keep your body from coming up and let the left arm fire through on its own.

Here's a simple cue I use: imagine a laser beam coming out of your chest, and that laser must stay locked onto the ball all the way until impact. It's not about where your head is — it's about your spine angle and your navel staying focused on the ball through the strike.

Work on this in three steps: first, drill the chest-laser cue to maintain spine angle; second, add awareness of keeping the hips folded through impact; third, once those feel natural, focus on letting the left arm release freely through the ball. Don't rush to step three until the first two are solid.

Avoid overusing your lower back and hips through impact the way young Tiger Woods did — that swing pattern leads to serious spinal injuries over time. I followed that model myself and ended up with severe spinal curvature, so I urge you not to repeat that mistake. Instead, use only a gentle, smooth lateral hip motion through the ball.

Don't try to lock your lower body and rotate only your upper body on the backswing — that creates excessive spinal torque and risks injury. Instead, think of turning your belly button to the right so that your entire body, upper and lower, rotates together as one unit. It's okay if your right knee straightens slightly and your left knee bends a little as a natural result of that full rotation.

Don't try to generate distance by violently twisting your upper and lower body against each other on the downswing — that destroys your ribs and discs. Instead, focus on shifting your weight: load it to your right heel on the backswing, then drive it forward toward your left toe through impact. All your power should flow into the ball through weight transfer, not body spin.

The goal is to concentrate all your force into one single point — the ball — rather than letting your body's rotational momentum leak past it. Think less about spinning your body and more about channeling your weight shift directly into the back of the ball. This is how you produce real distance with less physical effort and zero injury risk.

Hold the very end of the grip and feel the weight of the clubhead swinging freely. You must develop this sensation of head weight before you can generate real speed — without it, you're just swinging arms with no control over the clubhead.

Your hands and arms should move in a small, compact arc close to your body — but the clubhead travels in a large arc. If your arms are swinging wide and big, you will lose all sense of head weight. Keep the hand circle small and let the head do the work.

Don't snap or flip your wrists to feel the clubhead weight — instead, give a gentle upward lift of the wrists at the lowest point of the swing arc. Snapping is wrong; a soft, timed lift at the bottom is correct.

Wait until the club reaches its lowest point before applying that upward wrist lift. If you lift too early before the bottom of the arc, the head never properly accelerates and you lose all your speed.

Let your shoulder tension go completely. When your hands and arms move compactly inside your body, your shoulders naturally relax. If you try to swing big and wide, tension creeps into the shoulders and kills your speed.

Your arms and body must move as one connected unit — keep your elbows and triceps close to the sides of your chest throughout the swing. If your arms disconnect and go their own way, the clubhead becomes unpredictable and speed drops immediately.

On the backswing, don't reach your arms out long and away from your body. Keep the arms moving inside your body turn and simply rotate — the arms stay connected and the head rises naturally as a result of the body turn.

On the downswing, let the arms drop down and fall to the side first while you wait for the hands to reach the lowest point — do not immediately spin your body. Rotating too early breaks the arm-body connection and kills acceleration.

Instead of spinning in place, push your belly and hips toward the target to create real acceleration through the ball. This lower-body drive is what gives the clubhead the force to travel upward through impact — rotation alone without forward drive produces no real power.

Swing at only 60–70% of your arm effort and use your lower body to add more distance when needed. Swinging harder with your arms while disconnected from your body will send the ball anywhere — and will get you injured. Add power by using more lower body, not more arm force.
At address, position the ball so your sternum (chest center) is in the middle, with the ball aligned under your left armpit. This setup naturally promotes the upward strike angle the driver requires.

During your backswing turn, let your center of gravity shift slightly to the right — about 70% of your weight should load onto your right foot. This is what sets up a natural upward (upper blow) attack angle into the ball.

Once your weight is loaded on the right side at the top of the backswing, simply drop your arms and let the club swing through — your center of mass being behind the ball automatically creates an upward blow. Don't force it; the geometry does the work for you.

Keep your upper body and head staying back (right side) while your lower body drives toward the target. Shifting your weight to the front of your left foot is what allows you to push the club out to the side — the moment your upper body races ahead, the club gets thrown outside and you lose the upward strike.

Watch where your pressure goes in the downswing — pros shift dramatically onto the front of the left foot as they transition down. If your weight falls back to your heels early, your weight transfer stalls and you'll end up hitting behind the ball instead of through it.

If you try to fix coming over the top by just using your upper body, you create a messy mix of movements. Instead, keep the upper body quiet and right, and let the lower body lead the downswing — this separation is the fundamental engine of a consistent driver swing.

Practice this two-step drill: First, from the top of your backswing with 70% weight on the right foot, simply swing your arms and make solid contact using a side-blow (horizontal) feeling — prove to yourself you can hit it square from this position. Once that's consistent, add the lower body shift to the left on a 'one-two' count, letting the hips lead while the upper body stays back.

Stop trying to lead with your lower body or shoulders — start with your arms. At least 80% of your swing speed comes from three things: the arm-shoulder separation, the elbow movement, and the wrist action. Master these three first before worrying about anything else.

Practice drawing a large, consistent circle with your arms while keeping your shoulders as still as possible — think of your head as the fixed center point of a compass. This separation between your arms and shoulders generates enormous speed that most golfers completely ignore.

With your shoulder held quiet, focus on rotating your forearm and driving your elbow in a circular path. This elbow-driven movement creates a smaller circle than the full arm swing, but the speed it generates is tremendous — don't underestimate it.

Your wrist must trace a consistent circular arc where the thumb points toward the sky throughout the motion — not collapsing inward or flipping sideways. Practice this as if the clubhead is orbiting a fixed point in front of you, moving from below upward in one smooth loop.

Before picking up a club, practice swinging your bare hands and feel the weight of your own hands dropping — then when you grip the club, let that same sensation be amplified by the clubhead. If you find yourself forcing or steering the club, you've lost the feeling; relax your shoulders completely and let the head swing freely.

Imagine you're throwing a boomerang with your right hand or skimming a frisbee with your left — the goal is a natural, released throw, not a controlled push. This mental image helps you stop muscling the club and instead let the weight of the head do the work.

Don't copy tour pros using ground force or body-driven power until you can consistently feel the clubhead weight — that's the final stage, and you can't skip to it. It's like trying to drift a car before you've learned to drive in a straight line.

When practicing these arm, elbow, and wrist drills, drain all tension out of your shoulders — close your eyes and feel the weight of your hands falling naturally. Only when your shoulders are quiet can the three speed sources activate properly and deliver consistent contact.

Golf is a probability game, and your odds go up dramatically when the clubhead and your navel move together at all times. If your belly button is turning one way while the club goes another, your swing path changes and your consistency drops. Keep them connected throughout the entire swing.

The most critical zone in your downswing is from the top down to about hip height — this is where you must maintain your wrist hinge and rotate, not flip. The moment that hinge releases early, the clubhead points forward instead of at the ball, and you lose all your directional control. Maintain the hinge through that zone and rotate — don't let it spill out.

If you're hitting fat shots repeatedly, early wrist release in the downswing is almost always the cause. When the hinge breaks down too soon, the club bottoms out behind the ball. Practice maintaining that right wrist hinge and rotating through — don't dump it early.

If the clubface is open at impact and you're getting shank-like contact, check your backswing first — if the face is already fanned open going back, you're starting from a broken position. The face should be nearly square at the top, not pointing at the sky, and that only happens if your wrist hinge is set correctly from the start.

Think of your backswing like throwing a heavy dumbbell backward behind you — not lifting it up with your arms, but flicking it away using leverage. This creates the wrist hinge naturally and makes the club feel light. If you lift with your arms instead, the club stays heavy, your shoulders tighten up, and you lose all your speed.

A big backswing does not mean lifting your arms high — pros create width by using the hinge and leverage to flip the head behind them, keeping the swing compact and powerful. When you lift with your arms, you lose the ability to generate speed on the downswing. Keep the backswing short and use the hinge — three-quarter is more than enough if you do it right.

Most amateur golfers hit their maximum speed at the very start of the downswing, then decelerate into the ball — that is backwards. Save your speed, bring the club down slowly, and release everything just in front of the ball. For irons, think of your speed peak as being at your left foot; for driver, think right foot.

Picture your swing arc as being small on the backswing side and continuously growing longer through impact and into the follow-through. The circle is not round — it is elongated on the target side. Keep pushing and extending through the shot so the arc keeps getting bigger, never shorter.

Do not try to force your elbow into your body on the downswing — that actually causes the club to come over the top and steepen. Good players' arms drop in front of the body naturally because of how the body rotates; the arms lead, and the connection happens on its own. Focus on letting the arms fall in front of you, not gluing them to your side.

When your body rotates faster than your arms on the downswing, your elbow ends up behind you and you create severe off-center contact. The arms need to lead and stay in front of your body — practice feeling like the arms are dropping down first, and let the body follow rather than race ahead.

If you are getting golfer's elbow in your right arm, you are gripping too hard with your right hand — the right hand should be the lightest grip pressure of all. Squeezing with the right hand causes you to force the swing with that arm, which both damages your elbow and kills your swing path. Left hand holds firm; right hand stays soft.

You must understand exactly what you are practicing and why — if you just do drills because I told you to without understanding the reason, the next person who walks by and gives you advice will pull you off track immediately. Know what fault you are fixing, know why the drill works, and commit to it relentlessly. Golf rewards the smart and patient player.

If your takeaway feels too low and flat, imagine your knees are submerged in water and you are simply lifting the clubhead up out of the water to start your backswing. Feel like the club moves slightly outward and upward — almost a toe-out feeling — rather than dragging low along the ground.

When you keep the takeaway too low without cocking your wrists, the clubhead will droop and fall behind you. Allow natural wrist hinge to happen early in the backswing so the clubhead stays in front of you and the swing arc remains controlled.

Do not try to rotate your hips in place — that cue is wrong. Watch any PGA Tour pro and you will see their hips slide significantly toward the target, with the lead thigh almost pushing outside the stance line. Drive your hips left on the downswing; that lateral shift is the correct move.

If you spin your hips in place instead of shifting them toward the target, your right shoulder will come over the top and the ball will go left. Focus on moving the hips laterally first, then rotating, to keep the right shoulder low and the swing path from the inside.

A rising left shoulder through impact is not caused by restricted rotation — it is caused by pulling and lifting with the left arm instead of throwing the clubhead. Let the hips shift left, keep the upper body back, and feel the left shoulder drop and release naturally at impact rather than yanking it upward.

Many golfers tighten and pull the left arm through impact, which causes the left shoulder to rise and the shot to go left. Instead, feel as if you are throwing the clubhead outward and downward through the ball — the left shoulder should feel like it drops or thumps down, not lifts up.

The key feel you must develop is this: hips shift left, torso holds back slightly, and then the left arm and clubhead are thrown — not pulled — through the impact zone. That throwing sensation is what makes the right shoulder drop low like you see in every tour pro's follow-through.

For a 7-iron, position the ball in the center of your stance or just slightly left of center. Never place the ball to the right of center — this is a critical setup fundamental that affects everything that follows.

Your right elbow must point down toward your ribs at address — never let it flare out to the right. A flying right elbow is the number one reason golfers lose feel for the clubhead weight and destroy their swing plane before it even starts.
Don't pull the club back with your left arm alone. Instead, imagine your arms are connected to your belly button and initiate the takeaway by rotating your torso — the arms and body move as one unit.

After your torso rotates in the takeaway, complete the backswing by folding the right arm upward using a lever action — not by lifting your hands. Keep that right elbow tucked and fold it up to complete the backswing.

To start the downswing, never use your right shoulder to throw the club outward. Instead, lead with the left arm dropping the club straight down along the body — this is what we call the vertical drop, and most amateurs fail here by letting the right side take over.

Through impact, separate and rotate the left arm — keep the right shoulder passive and let the left arm lead the rotation. This left-arm-led rotation is the key to squaring the face and generating real power.

After impact, fold the left arm through the follow-through — don't let it stay straight and push outward. This folding action is what creates the feeling of centrifugal force and lets you feel the weight of the clubhead, which is essential for consistent ball striking.

If you're trying to hit harder with your right arm, the ball will go left and your swing will break down. Build left-arm strength and trust a left-arm-led swing — power comes from centrifugal force and clubhead weight, not from muscling it with the right arm.
Don't just swing and walk away — hold your finish and actually check it. Your finish position tells you exactly what went wrong during the swing, so use it as a diagnostic tool every single time.

At the finish, your right shoulder should be lower than your left — not higher. If your right shoulder is up at the finish, that means you forced power through the downswing with your right side, which causes an over-the-top or steep attack angle.

Check your right shoe at the finish — if the toe box is crushed or crumpled inward, you've spun out and failed to transfer your weight properly. Your right foot should be balanced on the toe, not collapsed, which confirms your hips rotated correctly through the shot.

The spine angle you set at address must be maintained all the way from the backswing through impact and into the finish. The moment that angle breaks down, your right shoulder rises and everything else falls apart.

I know everyone says 'feel the weight of the clubhead' and 'relax on the downswing,' but if you can't do that yet, check your finish instead — if there's tension in your finish, it was there in your downswing. Let the finish reveal the problem rather than trying to feel it mid-swing.

Hold your finish until the ball lands — this isn't just an old coach's habit, it forces your body to prepare for a balanced, complete swing from the very start. When your swing is truly working, your finish will feel natural and effortless.

When you draw your swing circle to the right at 45 degrees, most golfers instinctively stand up out of their posture out of fear. Push your hips back and keep your spine tilted forward throughout the entire motion. If your spine rises up, you've already lost the swing.

Most golfers flip or reverse their body at impact because the swing is going to the right and their instincts tell them to correct it. Don't flip — keep your spine angle down and let the circle stay to the right. Trust the path and fight that instinct.

Golfers who pull their elbow inward toward their body at impact are actually killing their centrifugal force. To generate real power, your left armpit should feel like it's dropping downward through the swing — that dropping sensation is how you feel the weight of the clubhead and use centrifugal force correctly.

If your swing direction comes too far around toward the ball, your armpit stays attached to your body and you get a chicken-wing follow-through. Swing out to the right at 45 degrees so your armpit naturally drops away from your body and centrifugal force is fully released.

If you try to keep your left arm completely straight while drawing the circle to the right, your shoulder gets too tense and the circle ends up pulling inward. Your left arm must be allowed to fold naturally once your hands pass chest height — that fold is what keeps the circle on the correct arc.

As your hands pass the level of your sternum in the follow-through, your left arm should fold so that your left elbow stays in front of your face — never flaring outward. At the same time, your right wrist should be bent back so that the club rests against your left trapezius muscle. That is the correct finish position.

Through impact and into the follow-through, keep your left hand back facing the target for as long as possible. Don't let it flip or rotate over early. The back of your left hand should still be pointing at the target when your hands reach chest height.

Think of your right hand as wiping a table diagonally in front of you — not straight ahead, but on a slight diagonal matching your swing path. If you wipe straight forward, your right armpit opens outward and you lose centrifugal force. Wipe diagonally and let your right palm finish facing the sky.

Choke down slightly on the driver grip and practice drawing a circle in the air with your arms — but place that circle to your right at about 45 degrees, not straight in front of you. Use arms only at first with no body rotation. This is the foundational drill you must master before adding anything else.

Once you can consistently swing the circle to the right with your right palm finishing skyward and your left hand staying face-up toward the target, add a small rotation to hit the ball. This will naturally produce a high draw — which travels further than a fade because of the forward spin and reduced backspin.

If you're still chasing a fade, understand that a draw will fly about 20 meters farther than your current fade. The natural swing arc of a golf club — with the ball positioned in front of you — already produces draw spin. Fighting that to hit a fade costs you distance without a meaningful scoring benefit for most golfers.

Place a ruler on your putting mat, set the ball over the hole in the ruler, and roll it straight to the end of the 1-meter ruler. This drill eliminates excess hand rotation and teaches you to roll the ball on a pure, straight line. Even a small mis-strike will knock the ball off the ruler, so it gives you instant feedback.

Make sure you complete your backswing rotation fully. When your shoulder turn is too short, the ball will consistently go left. Rotate your shoulders fully so you feel a real coil — that full turn is what sets up a powerful, accurate downswing.

Place a coin on the ground about one ball-width behind the ball, and commit 100% to not hitting it. This drill trains you to strike the ball first instead of the ground. Keep repeating this — it feels easy at first, but you'll hit that coin more than you think.

After your backswing, transfer all of your weight to your left side and stay there — support everything on your left foot through and after impact. If your weight falls back to the right side, the ball will start going right and you'll lose control of your shot shape.

When your backswing rotation is too short, your body is forced to stand up and block through impact just to reach the ball — you simply cannot rotate through properly from that position. A full, free backswing turn is what allows a smooth, uninhibited downswing rotation.

Do not confuse shifting your weight to the left with opening your left shoulder early. When your left shoulder opens too soon, your right arm comes through first and causes a scooping, belly-hit strike. Keep the left shoulder closed longer while driving your weight left — those are two completely different feelings.

Check your hip alignment at address — if your hips are already rotated open toward the target, you are making your backswing rotation much harder than it needs to be. Set your hips square at address so you only need a normal amount of turn to reach a full backswing position.

Use an impact trainer to feel the correct wrist bow position at impact — practice feeling the left wrist rotating into that bowed position during the backswing so that coming through impact it happens naturally. Once you know that feeling with a light trainer, you can work toward replicating it with a full-weight club.

On the driver, never swing at 100%. Always swing at 70% and focus on keeping the ball in play rather than chasing distance. The mindset should be 'get it on the green,' not 'hit it as far as possible.'

On the course, keeping the ball alive is always your number one priority — distance comes second. Even mishits can end up in good positions, so stay committed to a controlled, managed swing every single time.
On approach shots, never try to force the ball at the pin. It is perfectly fine to be slightly short — brush the ground softly and let the club do the work, and the ball won't run away from you.
The foundation of a good approach shot is rhythm and tempo — get those two things right and the ball will behave. Stay smooth, stay patient, and stop trying to smash it.

With short irons, consciously reduce the amount of body rotation through impact. Too much rotation on short irons causes the face to close too early, sending the ball left — dial it back and stay controlled.

Before every round, always test the green speed and spend time on putting practice. Putting is the one area where amateurs can most realistically match professionals, because it is built on feel and repetition, not raw athleticism.

When the pin is in a difficult position, adjust your target and club selection accordingly — for example, if the pin is front, play for the front edge or even slightly short rather than flying it past. Course management beats hero shots every time.

In the downswing, release your wrists vertically — letting them unhinge up and down — while simultaneously driving your hands toward the ball. The release itself is not the problem; the problem is when your hands drift away from your body as they release. Keep the hands moving toward the ball as the wrists unhinge.

Most golfers try to drag the hands down with a locked wrist and then rotate, but this sends the clubhead outside and causes severe shanks or over-the-top strikes. Instead, release the wrists first, then rotate — this is the correct sequence that naturally produces a forward shaft lean at impact.

Shanks are almost always caused by pulling the club down with unreleased wrists and then rotating — this throws the hosel directly into the ball. Fix it by releasing the wrists vertically before you initiate body rotation, so the clubhead approaches from the inside rather than the outside.

Begin your body rotation only after your wrists have started to release and your hands have reached approximately hip height on the downswing. If you have good athleticism, start rotating from the hips at that point; if not, wait until your hands reach chest height before initiating the turn.

Do not deliberately try to bow or snap your lead wrist through impact — that is a result, not a cause. When you release correctly and rotate properly, the wrist will naturally bow on its own due to clubhead acceleration. Trying to force it will only cause you to lose feel for the clubhead weight and produce more over-the-top swings.

If you don't know how to release the wrists correctly, your body will instinctively stand up or fall back to get the club to the ball — leading to thin shots, fat shots, or topped shots. Learn the proper wrist release so your body can stay in posture and rotate through the ball correctly.

Practice the wall drill: stand facing a wall and slap the back of your hand against it, focusing on releasing the wrist vertically as your hand moves toward the wall. Repeat this motion — release, release, slap with the back of the hand — until you can feel the timing of the unhinging wrist combined with the hand moving forward. This drill trains the exact release pattern needed for a correct downswing.

The key to the correct downswing is separating the arms from the shoulders — the wrists release and the hands travel toward the ball independently, before the body fully rotates. This is what I call 'arm and shoulder separation,' and without it you cannot rotate your torso freely or hit the ball with any real power.

Stop only practicing your swing and start training where your clubhead actually lands. Place a piece of tape behind the ball and practice striking the ground in front of the ball — for irons, aim to drop the head about 10–15cm ahead of the ball. This is not a technique issue; it's a trainable skill that anyone can improve with repetition.

When you have a real ball in front of you, you'll notice your body tenses up and the clubhead stops dropping where you want it. Consciously release that tension, keep your head still, and swing with the same relaxed feeling as your practice swing — let the head fall to the target spot, not to the ball.

Before every shot on the course, take a confident practice swing behind the ball with the sole focus of feeling the clubhead drop in front of where the ball is. Then step in and replicate that exact feeling. On the course, stop worrying about your swing mechanics — think only about rhythm and where you want the head to land.

When hitting driver, focus on dropping the clubhead toward the right big toe area as your landing reference point. This internal image helps you bottom out the swing in the correct spot and promotes a consistent, powerful strike.

If you play a draw, aim at the far left edge of the safe landing zone and commit to starting the ball right, letting the draw bring it back to the target — this doubles the width of the course you can use. If you play a fade, do the opposite: aim right and start the ball left. Always practice with a clear, deliberate start-line in mind.

Every player must define their acceptable miss side and train their brain to always miss that way. As a draw player, I am very forgiving of a miss to the right but very intolerant of a miss left — so I practice scoring myself: right misses score points, center is zero, and left is a penalty. Train your miss to be predictable, and your scoring will improve immediately.

Place an alignment stick in front of you during practice and commit to starting every ball 15cm to one side of that stick — never straight at it. Pair this with vivid mental imagery of the ball's start direction and shape before every shot. Without a clear picture of the start line, you are just hitting balls, not training your ball flight.

Use a ruler or straight-edge on the ground at home and practice rolling the ball along it for at least 1 meter perfectly straight. Because the surface is smooth and unforgiving, even a slightly open or closed face will send the ball off line immediately — this sharpens your face awareness far more than a regular putting mat.

To compress the ball like a pro, set up with your weight on your left side and your head behind the ball. From here, feel like the left hand is simply scraping forward through impact — the club should travel straight or slightly toward one o'clock, never flipping outward. When you do this correctly, you'll hear a sharp, solid 'thwack' at impact, like hitting a rice cake.

Do not use your wrists to hit the ball. The moment you flip your wrists, your left shoulder stalls, your hand speed slows down, and the clubhead takes over — killing all compression. Keep the left arm moving through on a consistent path and let the hands exit quickly without any wrist break.

A true forward shaft lean at impact means your hands are moving faster than the clubhead — not the other way around. The instant your hands stop and the wrists flip, the head accelerates but hand speed drops. Keep your hands driving forward through the zone so the shaft stays leaning toward the target at impact.

Set your spine angle at address by nudging your hips slightly to the side, and then protect that angle throughout the entire swing. If your spine angle collapses or shifts, you lose the foundation for solid contact. Keep your head as still as possible and rotate around a fixed axis — think of it as gently carrying a baby on your back as you turn.

Start your setup with about 60% of your weight on the left side, and do not let it drift to the right during the backswing. A slight reverse weight pattern — where the upper body tilts right while the hips stay left — is fine, keeping you around 50/50 or 60/40 at the top. What you must avoid is letting the hips slide right and pushing your weight to 70% or more on the trail side.

If the club keeps coming from outside to inside, you will never produce that compressed, penetrating ball flight. Practice the left-hand-only drill — grip with just the left hand, weight left, head behind the ball — and scrape the ground 5 cm in front of the ball repeatedly. This trains the club to approach from the inside and creates true compression.

Here is the drill: hold the club with your left hand only, load your weight to the left, place your head behind the ball, and maintain your spine angle. Without using your wrist, repeatedly brush the ground about 5 cm ahead of the ball in a straight or slightly one-o'clock direction. Once you feel the compression in this drill, add a backswing and transfer that same sensation into your full iron swing.

One lucky long shot means nothing in golf. What matters is consistency — if your average is 130m, you need to hit 130m every single time. Chase repeatability over raw distance, and the scoring will take care of itself.

If you're overswinging, it's almost always because the arms are doing the lifting — they flash up independently of the body. Stop initiating the backswing with your arms or shoulders. Instead, let your torso start the movement first, and let the arms simply follow the body's rotation.

Think of your belly button as the leader of your backswing. Your navel rotates to the right first, and the club is pulled along by that rotation — you are not lifting the club with your hands. Feel the weight of the clubhead moving on its own as your core turns.

Once your torso has initiated the turn, the only job your arms have is to fold the right elbow — nothing more. It's not a lifting feeling or a pulling-away feeling. Think of it like hoisting a heavy dumbbell onto your shoulder, or throwing a sack of rice up onto your back. The arms fold, they don't lift.

When you first shorten your backswing, it will feel powerless and weak — that's completely normal. Don't fight that feeling and don't try to force acceleration to compensate. Embrace the feeling of softness at the top; that's your signal that you're doing it right.

Instead of thinking about hitting hard, imagine you've placed a bag of rice on your shoulder at the top of the backswing — and all you're going to do is let that weight drop. Feel the heaviness of the clubhead, load it, then simply release that weight. That mental image will give you effortless power without forcing the swing.

When your arms lead the backswing and you overswing, the downswing becomes rushed and the body races ahead — that's what causes topped shots and shots that fly too high with no compression. Fix the backswing by leading with the torso, and you'll start compressing the ball properly with real energy transfer at impact.
In the downswing, drop your arms straight down vertically — don't throw them outward. If your arms swing to the outside, the club arc widens and you'll almost always hit fat shots.

At the top of your backswing, your right elbow should point down toward the ground — like you're holding a tray underneath it. If the elbow flares out to the side, your swing plane will shift outside and you'll lose your inside-out path.

Make a full 90-degree shoulder turn in the backswing and ensure your hands are behind your right heel at the top. A reverse pivot forces you to compensate on the way down, which kills both accuracy and club speed.

Don't actively try to release the club — just drop your arms down and let the weight of the clubhead do the work. The moment you cast or throw the club outward with your hands, you destroy any chance of a proper downward strike.

To hit a true downward blow with your irons, the clubshaft must be pointing well behind you as you start the downswing — much further back than it feels natural. Your body rotation will square the face automatically, so trust the feeling and commit to the inside path.

After you drop your arms down, shift your weight aggressively to the left side so your body arrives at impact before the clubhead does. This sequencing — arms drop, body shifts left — is what creates a proper downward blow and transfers the full weight of the head into the ball.

Keep your right arm in front of your chest throughout the backswing — your shoulder blade should stay tucked inward, not pulled behind you. The moment the right arm drifts behind the body, your downswing path is compromised before it even starts.

Stop trying to hit the ball with your shoulder and arm strength — that's the root of the problem. When you swing with pure muscle tension, letting go of that tension leaves you with nothing. Instead, feel your shoulders drop and release naturally, letting the weight of the club do the work.

Think of holding a heavy ball and dropping it to the ground — not throwing it with force, but releasing its weight. That's the feeling you want in your swing: let the weight fall, don't muscle it down. When your shoulder relaxes and you stop forcing it, you'll actually generate more speed.

If you're losing distance when you try to relax, don't panic — that's Stage 1, and it means you're on the right track. Focus entirely on releasing tension first, not on speed or distance. Speed comes later, once your body learns the feeling of a truly relaxed swing.

Give one sharp release impulse at the right moment — like a quick 'tang' — then let go completely and let the double pendulum effect do its job. The clubhead will whip past your hands on its own, generating centrifugal force and real speed without you forcing it.

If you're standing up through the ball, it means you're still trying to hit with your body instead of releasing the club. Keep your posture through impact — the goal is a sharp release of the hands and club, not a lunge with your torso.

If the ball is consistently going left, your shoulders are rushing and getting ahead of the release. Feel like you're throwing the club out to the side — not across your body — and let the release happen later and further out in front of you.

If the ball keeps going right, you haven't fully released the tension yet — you're still holding on through impact out of fear, which keeps the face open and causes a cut or push. Trust the release: let the head rotate and turn over freely as you let go.

If you're seeing a chicken wing in your follow-through, you still have too much tension in your arms — go back to basics and practice releasing all muscle tension first before adding any snap or speed. A true release will straighten and extend the arms naturally through the shot.

On the downswing, your right shoulder is coming out too early — we need to fix that first before anything else. Keep the right shoulder back and let the arms separate from the body as you come through. Once the crossover at the top is corrected, the shoulder dumping will naturally improve.

Your backswing is going across the line — the club is too high and crossing over at the top. This needs to be corrected first, because it is the root cause of the shoulder lunging on the downswing. Focus on keeping the backswing on plane before worrying about anything else.

Take the tension out of your swing — feel loose and comfortable before you even start. A tight, stiff swing produces inconsistent contact, while a relaxed swing produces smooth, consistent results. If you are tense, you cannot feel or correct anything.

On your backswing, feel like your arms are staying close to your hips — keep the takeaway low and under control. Imagine your hands staying low and trailing behind you rather than lifting up steeply. Stop at the top and check your position before swinging through.

If your trail elbow is flaring out like a chicken wing, focus on keeping the elbow tucking inward — but do not clamp the armpit shut at the same time. The key distinction is: elbow in, but armpit open. Confusing these two feelings is what causes the chicken wing in the first place.

Your lower body is drifting backward on the backswing, which causes you to hit the ball with your weight still behind the ball — producing topped shots. On the downswing, use your right knee to gently push forward and transfer your weight to the left side. Grip the ground with your left toes to stay stable as you shift.

Keep your head fixed through impact — your head is moving too much, which is causing you to top the ball. Practice keeping your head still while letting your hands release through the shot. A stable head gives you a consistent strike point.

Do not wait until impact to start rotating your forearms — begin the rotation from when the club is level with your right thigh on the downswing. Starting the rotation from the right thigh will bring the clubface back to square at impact naturally. If you try to rotate at the ball, you will always be too late.

Your left shoulder and arms are moving together as one unit, which kills your rotation. Focus on separating the left shoulder away from the chin on the downswing while keeping the right shoulder back. Let your arms travel away from the body independently rather than dragging everything together.

Do not give a student too many swing thoughts at once — it shuts them down mentally and physically. Pick the one or two most important faults and build confidence from there. A relaxed, encouraged student learns and improves far faster than one who is overwhelmed.

After impact, completely release all tension — imagine throwing the clubhead away like you're tossing it to the ground. Your arms should feel like they're stretching out from your body, not gripping tighter through the ball.

When you try to swing the club down to the ground, don't let your body drop with it — keep your chin up and let your arms do the work. The feeling should be your arms extending and releasing freely, not your whole torso collapsing downward.

If you swing with a tight grip, you risk elbow injury — but if you release tension fully after impact, there is no strain on the elbow at all. Just let the club go loose and fall wherever it wants after the strike.

Draw a line on the ground and practice dropping the clubhead consistently just in front of that line — like a sushi master who grabs the exact same amount of rice every time. Once you can reliably control where the club drops, the game becomes incredibly simple.

Before you ever hit a ball, master the feeling through practice swings — you get more feedback from practice swings than from actually hitting. Think of the ball as invisible and focus only on dropping the club to the right spot on the ground.

Don't try to manually force the L-to-L (lag-to-lag) follow-through position — when you fully release tension after impact, the L2L shape happens automatically. Stop chasing the position and chase the feeling of release instead.

If you feel like you're losing distance, your instinct will be to swing harder — but that only makes things worse. Do this release drill consistently for two weeks and you will naturally recover, and even increase, your distance without forcing anything.

Release all tension from your upper body before you swing. A tight upper body is the number one reason golfers struggle near hazards — let your arms and shoulders go soft, then let your lower body do the work.
Drive the swing with active hip rotation and weight transfer, not your hands or arms. Keep your head steady, push through with your hips, and let the body turn carry the club through the ball.

For short approach shots, memorize these swing size benchmarks: 30m = hip height, 40m = waist height, 50m = chest height, 60m = shoulder height. Don't guess — match your body rotation to the distance, and the ball will land softly every time.
Think of your arms and body as one unit during approach shots. Instead of trying to hit the ball with the clubhead, focus on rotating your whole body together — the club just goes along for the ride.

Never use your wrists on approach shots — scooping and flipping are the worst things you can do around the green. Keep your wrists passive and quiet throughout the entire swing; let body rotation do the work instead.

What many golfers think is forearm rotation is actually just a wrist flip — and they are not the same thing. True rotation means your left hand back faces the ground through impact, not curling or breaking at the wrist.

To square the clubface correctly, imagine reaching out to shake hands with a target in front of you — when your right hand makes that handshake motion, the clubface naturally matches your spine angle at impact. Never let the face fall open.

On every approach shot, rotate your right hip forward and imagine shaking hands with a target out in front of you. Your arms should never work alone — the hip turn leads, and the hands simply follow along.

Never let your upper body lunge or rush at the ball with the driver. The driver requires the shallowest angle of attack of any club, and if your upper body fires first, you'll make the swing too steep and lose solid contact. Be patient — let your body wait and your arms do the work.

With the driver, train yourself to take the right shoulder completely out of the equation. Imagine your left hand is fixed in place and your right hand simply fires past it — that explosive arm extension through impact is what you're after, not a push from the right shoulder.

Your swing arc must stay as wide as possible on the downswing — never let the arc shrink. Feel like the clubhead is fully released and heavy as it swings through, maximizing the arc so the head sweeps the ball rather than hitting down on it.

If you're hitting fat shots, check whether your head is swaying too far to the right during the backswing. Your head should stay stable — focus on rotating your body, not sliding it, so you return to the same position at impact.

Fat shots with the driver are almost always caused by the body rising up too early in the downswing out of fear of hitting the ground behind the ball. Maintain your spine angle all the way through impact — stay down, be patient, and just throw the arms through. If your spine angle holds, you simply cannot hit it fat.

In the follow-through, your right elbow must point down toward the ground — never let it rotate outward or 'chicken wing' away from your body. The moment that right elbow turns over, you've lost your ability to drive the ball properly with the driver.

Release all tension from your shoulders and simply throw your arms — when your arms move freely, your body will rotate naturally on its own. Squeezing with your shoulders causes the body to block and restrict rotation, but a relaxed arm swing will always pull the body through automatically.

The key feel for a great driver swing is that the clubhead crosses your body first — not your hands leading the way. Imagine the head is so heavy that it swings across and past you, and you are just along for the ride. If you can feel that heavy, free-releasing clubhead, you've found the right motion.

Keep your left shoulder closed through the swing — the moment it opens up, the ball will go left every time. I noticed this myself on camera today: as soon as my left shoulder flew open, I lost the shot. Just focus on blocking that left shoulder and everything straightens out.

Don't let your lower body thrust forward — avoid 'belly-bumping' through the shot. Keep the left shoulder closed and let the lower body clear naturally without lunging. That combination alone will give you much more consistent contact.

On a downhill lie, don't try to scoop or lift the ball — accept that it will fly low and just swing down and through. The moment you try to help it up, you create a mis-hit. Trust the loft, swing down the slope, and take the low trajectory.

Stop letting your shoulders do all the work. Think 'swing with your back to the target' — lead with rotation, not with the arms and shoulders firing independently. When I focused on turning my back to the target first, my ball-striking improved immediately.

Consistency comes from showing up regularly, not from marathon sessions. My goal is 100 balls a day, five days a week — that steady rhythm is enough to maintain your feel and improve faster than you think. Field rounds at least twice a month are also essential to translate range work into real scoring.

On chip shots around the green, always pick a specific landing spot first and commit to hitting it. Pick the point where you want the ball to land and let it release to the hole — if you land it in the right zone, the ball will do the rest of the work for you.

Fear is what makes your shoulder open up — you get tense and your body bails out of the shot. Trust the swing you've built: close the shoulder, commit through the ball, and stop guarding against a miss. The more you protect, the worse it gets.

You don't need to use your body to generate distance — your arms are your primary power source. Master arm swing first, and only add body rotation later to control shot shape. Chasing an extra 6-10 meters with body mechanics before you own your arm swing will cost you far more strokes on the course.

Your arms must travel in a straight line through the swing — think of them swinging along a single direct path rather than looping in or out. Any deviation where you pull the hands outward or reroute them behind you will create deceleration and kill your speed. Make sure your backswing rotation is full enough so that your downswing arm path stays straight without any rerouting.

The goal is to reach 100% speed at impact, then let the clubhead decelerate naturally like snapping a towel — your arms slow down and the head whips through. If you keep pushing with your arms past impact, you're using arm strength instead of clubhead weight, and you'll lose both speed and feel. Practice stopping a flexible stick or training aid right at the impact zone and feel the tip flick forward on its own.

Don't try to push the club through to the finish with arm force — instead, release at impact and let the weight of the clubhead carry you into the follow-through. Think of it as throwing the head out and letting the rebound pull you into your finish. The club does the work; your job is to accelerate to impact and then get out of the way.

If you've only learned 20% of how to use your arms and you start adding body movement on top of that, you'll make things much worse. Get to 100% arm proficiency first — everyone, no matter how uncoordinated, can do this. Once your arm swing is solid, then and only then should you explore adding lower body movement for extra distance.

If your right foot is wider than your shoulder width without your right shoulder following, you will sway instead of rotate on the backswing. When you widen your stance for the driver, your right shoulder must move out with your right foot so the body stays aligned. A wide stance with only the feet causes a lateral sway that kills both power and solid contact.

At address for the driver, load your weight roughly 70-80% onto your right side so that when you simply rotate back, your weight naturally reaches 80-90% on the right foot at the top of the backswing. This pre-loaded position makes it much easier to deliver an upward, ascending strike through impact. Without this setup, hitting up on the ball becomes nearly impossible.

On the downswing, your left shoulder should be rising upward, not dropping down toward the ball. As your weight shifts left, feel your left shoulder lifting and your left ribcage stretching and expanding. This upward shoulder movement keeps your head behind the ball and creates the ascending angle of attack you need for maximum driver distance.

During the downswing, you should feel the inner bone on the ball of your right foot pressing firmly into the ground. If your downswing is correct, this pressure will happen naturally and is your confirmation that you are rotating properly rather than sliding. Use this sensation as your feedback cue — no pressure means something has gone wrong in the sequence.

Instead of thinking about hitting the ball, imagine swinging the clubhead all the way up onto your left trapezius muscle after impact — just let it land there. This mental image keeps the clubhead accelerating continuously through the entire swing arc rather than decelerating at the ball. Any change in path or intention at impact instantly kills clubhead speed.

After impact, your right leg should push through fully so that your weight completes its transfer to the left side — never let your weight hang back on the right foot with your right leg kicking forward independently. The finish should feel like your right leg drove the rotation all the way through, with the shaft even wrapping around and touching your back as long hitters do. Weight staying back is the enemy of both distance and consistency.

Stop trying to scoop the ball out of the bunker with your wrists — that's the old V-swing method and it kills your consistency. Instead, keep the face open at address and swing through with a shallow, low-and-long motion, maintaining that same face angle from backswing all the way through impact. If you just hold that open face and don't rotate it closed, you'll escape the bunker almost every time.

Don't swing steep and aggressive into a bunker — swing low and shallow, like you're brushing the turf on an approach shot. Think of it as a U-shape swing, not a V-shape. A shallow entry lets the bounce of the club do the work and gives you a much more consistent contact point.

One of the biggest mistakes I see is letting the clubface rotate closed through impact in the bunker. Open the face at address, and keep your palm facing upward through the follow-through — if your palm doesn't rotate over, the face won't close, and the ball will come out high and soft every time.

Keep your weight on your left side throughout the entire bunker shot — set it there at address and leave it there. The moment your weight shifts to your right foot, you'll either skull the ball or chunk it. Weight left, stay left.

For bunker shots, open your clubface first, then set your stance slightly open by dropping your left foot back — this compensates for the open face so the ball still flies at your target. You don't need an extreme open stance, just enough to match the face angle.

Play the ball off your left foot in the bunker and dig your feet into the sand for stability. This setup alone — weight left, ball forward, feet planted — gives you the foundation for a consistent bunker shot before you even swing.

Amateur golfers consistently swing too timidly in the bunker — you need to swing 2 to 2.5 times harder than you think for the distance you want. Because the face is open and the club is entering sand, not hitting the ball directly, you lose a massive amount of energy, so commit to a full, confident swing. A topped ball that flies too far is a better miss than a scared decel swing that leaves you in the bunker.

The whole principle of the bunker shot is using the bounce of the wedge — enter the sand about 1cm behind the ball with the bounce, not the leading edge. Imagine you're scooping up sand and throwing it onto the green toward the hole; let the sand carry the ball out, not the clubhead hitting the ball directly.

If your backswing is too long, it's likely because you're missing the pressing and pushing force from your left arm. When I shortened my backswing by focusing on pushing the left arm low and long, my distance actually increased and my strike rate improved dramatically. A compact, controlled backswing creates more body tension and coil than an overswing ever will.

To get proper shoulder and torso rotation, focus on pressing and pushing your left arm out low and long during the takeaway. When you push the left arm outward with intention, your shoulders have no choice but to rotate fully. You'll feel your body wind up tight — that's the feeling you're looking for.

Don't push both arms forward during the backswing — if your right arm also pushes outward, it will cause a chicken wing and collapse your structure. Instead, think of your right arm as flipping a phone screen to show someone beside you. This naturally folds the right elbow down and keeps it connected.

One of the worst habits I had was lifting the club with only my arms, with zero shoulder turn or body tension. This gives you no power and no consistency. Make sure the left arm is actively pushing and pressing to trigger the body rotation — never just pick the club up with your arms alone.

To build a wide, efficient backswing arc, keep pressing and extending the left arm low and long throughout the takeaway while simultaneously folding the right elbow downward. This combination maximizes your arc width while keeping the swing on the correct plane, setting you up perfectly for a down-blow strike.

When your backswing is built correctly — left arm pressing and pushing, right elbow folding down — the club will naturally return on the same path it went back on. This on-plane movement is what gives you that satisfying feeling of the club dropping back down the exact same groove, leading to pure contact and consistent downward strikes.

If the new backswing sensation feels strange, try closing your eyes and rehearsing it slowly without a club. Feel the left arm pushing and extending, then sense the right arm folding. When you hit that 'locked in' position where you physically cannot go further back, that's the correct top of your backswing — now just hit from there.

Swinging harder does not mean the ball goes farther. I hit 276 meters with full effort and then again with almost no tension — the distance was identical. Stop trying to muscle the ball and focus on the quality of your motion instead.

If I could only practice one thing for the driver, it would be this: backswing up, then drop the left arm down. Backswing, drop — backswing, drop. Then rotate. Repeat this sequence over and over until it becomes automatic.

During the backswing, your right shoulder blade should feel like it is dropping down, not rising up. Imagine hanging from a pull-up bar — feel how your shoulder blades sink under your own weight. That sinking sensation in the right scapula is exactly what you need at the top of your backswing.

Think of cradling a tray from underneath rather than lifting it from above. When you feel like you are supporting the club from below during the backswing, your right shoulder blade drops naturally into the correct position — and that sets you up to drop the club down into the downswing instead of casting it over the top.

Do not start your body rotation until the club has already begun to drop. If your shoulder blade is still elevated and you rotate early, the club will come over the top and cut across the ball. The sequence must be: drop first, then rotate.

The driver is the longest and lightest-headed club in the bag — around 200g versus nearly 300g for an iron. Because the head is so light, it does not naturally want to fall, which makes the drop feel unfamiliar and even scary. You have to train yourself to be comfortable with that falling sensation; only then will the driver become an easy club to hit.

Use your iron swings to fix your overall technique, but when you practice the driver separately, focus on just one thing: the feel of dropping the left arm. Fix the full swing with irons, and train the drop with the driver.

Don't underestimate the power of your arms — even with your lower body completely restricted, proper arm swing alone can generate impressive distance. Focus on developing fast, free arm speed first, before worrying about body rotation. Pros maintain distance well into their 70s precisely because they use their arms so efficiently.

If you squeeze the club hard through transition and try to muscle it, you'll lose significant distance — think around 140m versus 156m with a relaxed swing. Release the tension and let the club swing freely instead of forcing it with grip pressure. A loose, whipping arm swing will always outperform a tight, forced one.

Think of swinging the club like a yo-yo — hold it with your right hand only, relax your shoulder completely, and swing it in a circle toward the target, feeling the head naturally lag behind and then release. You should feel a distinct 'thud' sensation as the head is thrown out at the bottom of the arc. If you can't feel the clubhead weight, you won't be able to use your arms correctly.

Every club has a natural shaft angle at address, and you must swing along that plane to maximize speed — the driver lies flat so you should feel like you're swinging almost horizontally forward, while a 7-iron sits more upright so you swing more vertically. Most golfers do the opposite: they swing the driver too steeply and the wedge too shallow, which kills clubhead speed. Match your swing direction to the club's natural plane angle and you'll unlock much more effortless power.

When hitting a driver, imagine the ball is sitting on an uphill lie in front of you — this mental image will naturally encourage a shallower, more horizontal swing path. Swinging along a flatter plane keeps speed from bleeding off and promotes an in-to-out path that produces a healthy draw. If the ball is drifting left, increase your body rotation on the backswing and the trajectory and distance will both improve.

On the backswing, don't use your arms to lift the club — instead, keep your hands passive and simply rotate your torso, letting your spine angle dictate the natural takeaway path. With a driver your flatter spine angle will automatically create a shallow takeaway, and with an iron your steeper address position will create a slightly more upright path. Trust the rotation and stop trying to steer the club into position with your hands.
